item.title: The world that forgot to come back. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There is a child in Cox’s Bazar who has never known any home but a camp. She was born somewhere between bamboo and tarpaulin to parents who crossed jungles and rivers in the dark of August 2017.
She is nine years old now. She has never seen Rakhine State. She does not know what citizenship feels like. And, by any official count, she remains a “temporary” presence in Bangladesh.
This August marks nine years since the most violent chapter of the Rohingya exodus. More than 723,000 people crossed into Bangladesh after August 25, 2017, fleeing what the United Nations described as textbook ethnic cleansing.
According to UNHCR Bangladesh, the country now hosts more than 1.2 million Rohingya, over 90% of the world’s displaced Rohingya population, in 33 camps in Cox’s Bazar and on Bhashan Char. More than half are under 18.
Bangladesh opened its borders and thereby absorbed enormous pressure on Cox’s Bazar’s land, forests, water, and livelihoods. Host communities watched resources increasingly favour the refugee response.
Bangladesh has consistently called for safe, dignified and voluntary repatriation; although Myanmar agreed in principle in early 2025 to accept 180,000 Rohingya initially, with another 70,000 under verification, the process has stalled amid the Arakan Army’s control of much of Rakhine State and Myanmar’s political turmoil.
The roadmap exists on paper. The road does not.
Bangladesh cannot integrate the Rohingya without risking permanence and weakening pressure for repatriation, cannot force them back into a country at war, and cannot sustain more than a million people indefinitely as international aid declines.
Compounding this is a structural vacuum: Bangladesh has no national refugee policy or domestic legal framework governing the status and rights of those it shelters.
A million people are being managed through humanitarian directives and improvised arrangements for what has become a decade-long presence. Meanwhile, the boundaries between “guest” and “neighbour” have inevitably begun to blur.
The most immediate threat is now the erosion of the humanitarian response itself.
In March 2025, the government of Bangladesh and the United Nations launched the 2025–26 Joint Response Plan, seeking $934.5 million to support 1.48 million people. By mid-year, it was only 21.7% funded. Food rations were reduced again, while schools and primary healthcare services faced closure.
More than 95% of Rohingya in Bangladesh depend entirely on humanitarian assistance for food, healthcare, and education. According to Unicef, a 27% budget loss led to the closure of approximately 2,800 schools in June 2025.
An International Rescue Committee survey found that 69% of refugee households reported children dropping out of school, while half said their children had been forced into labour. Only 2% of parents said they felt hopeful about their children’s futures.
These are not abstract statistics. They describe daily life for more than a million people living in fragile shelters on landslide-prone hills, waiting for aid in a country that is not theirs and a crisis that is no longer headline news.
The Rohingya funding crisis is part of a wider global humanitarian recession. International humanitarian assistance fell by nearly $5 billion in 2024, the largest single-year decline recorded. In 2025, funding for the UN’s global appeal was at its lowest in a decade, while humanitarians reached 25 million fewer people than the previous year.
Meanwhile, major crises, from Gaza and Sudan to Ukraine, Syria, Haiti, Yemen, the Democratic Republic of Congo and the Sahel, compete for political attention and scarce resources.
The Rohingya, stateless for decades before the 2017 violence, occupy an especially difficult position: Their crisis is neither urgent enough for the front page nor resolved enough to be forgotten.
There is another uncomfortable contradiction. For years, the humanitarian sector has championed localization, the principle that local and national organizations should lead responses in their own countries rather than serve as subcontractors to international organisations.
The Grand Bargain, agreed by major donors and aid organisations in 2016, committed to directing 25% of humanitarian funding to local actors by 2020. That target was missed; direct funding to local organisations has remained below 3% for years. As donor budgets shrink, this gap risks becoming structural.
Bangladesh has organizations with deep roots in the communities they serve, alongside the language, relationships, and contextual knowledge needed for effective humanitarian work. They do not need layers of intermediaries. They need resources, trust, and sustained investment in institutional capacity.
The ninth year therefore demands more than commemoration. It demands four honest conversations.
First, repatriation needs a diplomatic strategy.
With Rakhine State at war and much of it controlled by the Arakan Army, Bangladesh cannot negotiate alone. ASEAN, China, and the UN Security Council must find ways to engage relevant actors on conditions for return, or accept that repatriation is unlikely soon and plan accordingly. The Rohingya’s right to return means little without citizenship, safety, and a Myanmar willing to accept them.
Second, dignity cannot wait for return.
If repatriation is not imminent, the Rohingya need more than survival: livelihoods, accredited education, psychosocial support, protection from violence and trafficking, and greater space to develop their own leadership and civic institutions.
Third, funding must match the localization promise.
National organizations need direct, sustained funding, not layers of international intermediaries or short grant cycles, to build capacity and deliver effective, context-driven responses.
Fourth, host communities must be part of the solution.
Bangladesh’s generosity has placed significant pressure on Cox’s Bazar. A sustainable response must invest in local infrastructure, services, and livelihoods alongside those of the Rohingya. The two communities share one ecosystem; treating them accordingly is not charity, but logic.
Nine years after a night of fire and flight that much of the world has largely forgotten, more than a million people remain in limbo, waiting for schools to reopen, for rations to arrive in full, for safety, and for the chance to return with dignity.
For a generation of nine-year-olds, teenagers, and young adults who have known nothing but the camps, that wait is for something they cannot yet name: The first real day of a life that belongs to them.
Md Quamruzzaman is Head of Pooled Fund for Localization, Advocacy for Social Change, Brac and Fahmid Ahmed Khan is Localization Communication Expert, Brac.

item.description:
Muslims are not creating an 'Islamic Republic' in Britain. This is their home

Submitted by Soumaya Ghannoushi on Mon, 08/24/2026 - 15:37
Netanyahu's absurd comments reveal a deeply exclusionary idea of citizenship - one where visibility becomes demographic menace
Worshippers attend the East London Mosque on 9 August 2024 (Henry Nicholls/AFP)
On

A few days ago, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu offered a startling description of one of Israel’s oldest allies.

In an interview with Israeli Army Radio, Netanyahu referred to the “Islamic Republic of Britain”, describing the country as the “first Islamic republic to get a nuclear weapon”.

It was meant as a warning. But it revealed far more about the politics behind the phrase than about Britain itself.

Britain is a diverse democracy in which Muslims constitute around six percent of the population. Their growing visibility - in politics, culture, professional fields and public life - is the ordinary consequence of generations of settlement, citizenship and participation.

Yet in the politics of anti-Muslim alarmism, visibility is recast as domination, diversity as “Islamisation”, and participation as infiltration. The underlying proposition is a curious one: when Muslims become sufficiently visible in a democracy, democracy itself has somehow become Muslim.

The selectivity is telling. Britain recently had a practising Hindu prime minister, Rishi Sunak. Curiously, Netanyahu and his ideological allies detected no impending “Hinduisation of Britain”. There were no warnings that Westminster was becoming a Hindu republic.

Sunak was succeeded by Keir Starmer, whose wife is Jewish and whose children were raised within Jewish traditions. Again, no talk of the “Judaisation of Britain”, nor any speculation about a Jewish republic emerging on the banks of the Thames.

Britain is now led by Andy Burnham, a Catholic. So far, the “Catholicisation of Britain” has apparently escaped Netanyahu’s attention too.

Ethnic diversity

Yet introduce Muslims into precisely the same plural society, and the vocabulary abruptly changes. Muslim mayors, MPs, doctors, lawyers and voters become evidence not simply of participation, but of “Islamisation”. Their visibility becomes demographic menace; their political influence, infiltration.

Religious pluralism, it seems, remains religious pluralism - until the religion happens to be Islam.

The facts are considerably less dramatic. There are roughly four million Muslims in Britain. They remain a small minority within one of the most religiously and ethnically diverse societies in Europe. 

Integration does not mean becoming invisible. It does not mean abandoning one's faith, name, culture or political opinions

Britain has no remotely significant political movement seeking to establish an Islamic state. The fantasy of an impending caliphate belongs overwhelmingly to the imagination of those warning against it.

The British state, meanwhile, remains stubbornly British. Parliament has not been replaced by a shura council. British law has not been supplanted by Islamic law. Buckingham Palace has not become the seat of a caliph. The country’s institutions, constitution and political culture have not undergone some clandestine Islamic transformation.

What has changed is much simpler: British Muslims have become more visible.

They are doctors and teachers, lawyers and engineers, academics and journalists. They sit in parliament and local councils. They run businesses, work in hospitals, teach in universities, serve their communities and vote in elections. Their children and grandchildren speak English as their first language, and know Britain not as a temporary host country, but as home.

To portray this as evidence of an Islamic takeover is to confuse citizenship with conquest - and that confusion has a history.

Permanent foreignness

Islam is not a newcomer to the European story. For more than a millennium, Europe and the Muslim world have encountered one another through war, trade, scholarship, migration, diplomacy and cultural exchange.

Muslim civilisation flourished for centuries in al-Andalus. Arabs and Ottomans appeared repeatedly in the political imagination of Christian Europe. From Poitiers to Vienna, the Muslim “other” helped Europe define what it believed itself to be.

Islam was therefore never simply outside European history. It was one of the forces against which, and through interactions with which, Europe fashioned itself.

Exposed: The dirty campaign to paint Muslim MPs as anti-British
Read More »

After the Second World War, that relationship changed fundamentally. European countries rebuilding shattered economies drew workers from colonies and former colonies. Britain received migrants from South Asia and elsewhere; France from North Africa; other European states from their own spheres of colonial influence or labour recruitment. 

These men and women worked in factories, transport systems, hospitals and public services. They helped rebuild Europe, while frequently living at its social margins.

They settled. Their children were born, and then their grandchildren. The “migrant” became the citizen.

That transformation matters because much of today’s rhetoric remains trapped in the language of arrival, as though millions of Europeans of Muslim background had only just stepped off a boat and might at any moment be persuaded to return somewhere else.

But where, exactly, is a fourth-generation Londoner supposed to “return” to? Britain is home. That is the reality with which the politics of permanent foreignness struggles to contend.

Modern Britain is not a sealed cultural inheritance passed untouched from one generation to another. It is a society continually shaped by the people who inhabit it. Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, Sikh, secular and non-religious lives now overlap within the same national space.

And integration has never meant that minorities simply dissolve into an unchanged majority culture. It works both ways.

Societal evolution

Migrants and their descendants absorb the language, institutions, habits and sensibilities of the societies in which they live. Those societies, in turn, are changed by them: food, music, language, fashion, cities, political priorities, ideas of belonging - all of these things change.

This is not “Islamisation”. It is what societies do: they evolve.

The alternative is to imagine national identity as something preserved under glass, authentic only if protected from the contaminating presence of people who look different, worship differently or have different names.

That vision has always been historically dubious. In modern Britain, it is simply untenable.

There is, however, a political reason for portraying ordinary social change as civilisational danger.

Across Europe, sections of the populist and far right have discovered that Muslims make an extraordinarily useful political abstraction. Housing shortages, pressure on public services, economic insecurity, social fragmentation and failures of government can all be folded into a simpler story: the country is being taken away from you.

The Muslim then ceases to be a neighbour, colleague, surgeon, shopkeeper, teacher or fellow citizen, and becomes a symbol of national decline.

Netanyahu’s language belongs within this broader politics of threat. It is also politically convenient.

At a moment when Britain and other western governments face growing pressure over Israel’s conduct towards Palestinians, criticism can be answered not on its merits, but by questioning the societies producing it. Opposition to Israeli policy becomes evidence of Islamist influence; Muslim political participation becomes infiltration; demographic evolution becomes civilisational surrender.

The argument effectively turns democracy against itself.

Muslims are told to integrate. But when they integrate successfully, enter institutions, vote, organise and acquire political influence like other citizens, that very participation is offered as evidence that they have acquired too much power.

They are required to participate - but preferably without consequence.

Part of the story

This is why the phrase “Islamic Republic of Britain” deserves more than ridicule. Beneath its absurdity lies a deeply exclusionary idea of citizenship: that some citizens belong naturally to the nation, while others remain permanent guests whose political visibility requires explanation.

A Muslim can apparently be British - provided his/her Britishness remains sufficiently inconspicuous.

But citizenship does not work that way. A British Muslim elected to parliament is not evidence that Muslims have captured Britain. It is evidence that British Muslims vote and stand for election.

A Muslim doctor in the National Health Service is not evidence of Islamisation. A mosque beside a church, synagogue or temple is not evidence of conquest.

Britain is not becoming an Islamic republic. It is becoming what it has been becoming for generations: a more diverse version of itself

A Muslim family whose grandparents arrived from Pakistan, Bangladesh, India, Somalia or Morocco, does not become less British because they retain a religious inheritance alongside their national one.

Pluralism is not the disappearance of Britain. It is contemporary Britain - and the growing political presence of Muslims should be understood accordingly. As communities become established, educated and socially rooted, their political participation naturally increases. The same process has occurred repeatedly with minority communities across democratic societies.

There is nothing mysterious about it. The more interesting question is why Muslim participation so readily becomes a source of panic.

Perhaps this is because the controversy is not really about whether Muslims can integrate. It is about whether some people are prepared to accept what integration actually means.

Integration does not mean becoming invisible. It does not mean abandoning one’s faith, name, culture or political opinions. And it certainly does not mean forfeiting the right to influence the country of which one is a citizen.

It means belonging.

Britain is not becoming an Islamic republic. It is becoming what it has been becoming for generations: a more diverse version of itself.

Its Muslims are not standing outside that story. They are very much a part of it.

item.title: Supporting the media must be more than rhetoric. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The newly appointed Information and Broadcasting Minister Andaleeve Rahman’s pledge to support the media rather than control it is a welcome and encouraging commitment.
At a time when the relationship between the state and the press is under close scrutiny, recognizing the media as a pillar of democracy and acknowledging its role in exposing government failures and irregularities is an important step in the right direction.
The minister has also rightly distinguished between regulation and control: A functioning democracy needs reasonable regulation to uphold professional and ethical standards, but regulation must never become a means of restricting legitimate journalism, silencing criticism, or influencing editorial decisions.
The media’s responsibility is to inform the public, scrutinize those in power, and give citizens access to facts -- including those that are uncomfortable.
However, promises of press freedom ultimately mean little without corresponding action. Bangladesh has experienced enough instances where commitments to openness have been undermined by practices that constrain journalists and media organizations.
If the government is serious about establishing a new system, as the minister has suggested, this must include creating an environment where journalists can work without intimidation, harassment, or undue political pressure.
To that end, access to information should be facilitated, official communication should be transparent, and journalists should not have to fear repercussions for asking difficult questions or investigating matters of public interest.
There is also a need for institutional safeguards that ensure media freedom does not depend on the goodwill of any particular minister or government.
Strong laws, independent institutions, and clear protections for journalists are more meaningful than assurances alone.
While the minister’s words are certainly encouraging, the real test will come in the months ahead. If actions consistently match these promises, the government can help rebuild public trust and strengthen democratic institutions.
Until then, the country will rightly judge these commitments by what is done, not merely what is said.

item.title: The Rohingya crisis is reaching a breaking point. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Nine years after the mass exodus of Rohingya from Myanmar, Bangladesh continues to shoulder a responsibility that was never meant to be permanent.
More than a million Rohingya remain dependent on humanitarian assistance, while the prospect of returning home remains frustratingly distant.
As the crisis creeps up to a decade, it is difficult to avoid the conclusion that the international response has fallen far short of what is required.
Bangladesh has provided shelter and humanitarian support despite the enormous economic, social, and environmental pressures imposed on host communities, but this generosity cannot be allowed to become an excuse for international inaction.
The Rohingya have a right to return to their homeland, and Bangladesh has a right to expect that Myanmar take responsibility for creating the conditions necessary for their safe, dignified, and sustainable return.
Recent developments surrounding verification offer little reason for complacency. Myanmar has verified more than 300,000 refugees as former residents of Rakhine State, but the process remains painfully limited compared to the scale of the population in Bangladesh.
Security concerns and the continuing conflict in Rakhine further underline why repatriation cannot simply mean sending people back into another cycle of insecurity.
What has long been needed is sustained international pressure on Myanmar. Major powers, regional organizations, and the United Nations must make accountability central to their engagement with Myanmar.
Furthermore, those responsible for the atrocities that drove the Rohingya from their homes must face meaningful consequences, while Myanmar must be pressed to recognize the rights, citizenship, and security of the Rohingya.
At the same time, humanitarian funding must not be allowed to decline. Until repatriation becomes possible, Bangladesh cannot be expected to carry the financial and social burden alone.
Nine years is far too long for a temporary refuge to become a permanent existence.
The priority must now be immediate, voluntary, safe, and dignified repatriation -- and the international community must act with the urgency this crisis demands.

item.title: Is there any possibility for Rohingya repatriation?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Both the Rohingya and the people of Bangladesh have already heard a lot of promises and dialogues, and witnessed many initiatives to repatriate the Rohingya.
Soon, they realized that the unfulfilled promises and unrealized conversations simply increased the confidence of the Myanmar’s junta in continuing their atrocities against the Rohingya and plotting the game of trust traps.
August 25, 2026 is the ninth year of the Rohingya Genocide Remembrance. If we critically and objectively review the events that took place with the Rohingya in the past nine years, we see how the situation has deteriorated gradually, showing little or no hope for repatriation. Bangladesh could not repatriate a single Rohingya in the last nine years and rather, it kept accepting more Rohingya from Myanmar almost on a regular basis, even in 2026.
On the one hand, we could not show our strength to Myanmar, as well as to the rest of the world, by exercising bilateral or multilateral or track diplomacy. On the other hand, the “mighty” countries have continued showing interest in sending relief to the Rohingya in Bangladesh instead of standing beside Bangladesh to repatriate them, and investing more in trade with Myanmar.
Bangladesh has been dealing with refugees for over four decades without any national refugee policy. Time has come now to end this adhocism. In order to play bold and safe in this complicated field of Rohingya repatriation, the 11-member National Strategy Formulation Committee on Rohingya Affairs must remember a few points.
Utilizing the history of Rohingya political leaders
We have failed to explore and reveal the history, culture, and strong records of the existence of the Rohingya in Myanmar as an indigenous people of Myanmar, particularly of Arakan.
Their history has been preserved in international museums and archives, although Myanmar demolished their histories from the record of Myanmar.
Bangladesh could have utilized the history of the Rohingya political leaders and MPs in Myanmar such as Sultan Ahmed who won from Maungdaw-1 constituency in 1951 general election, both Nur Ahmed (Tin Maung) who won from Buthidang-2 and U Fazal Ahmed who won from Maungdaw-2 contested in 1990 general election, and many other to let the world know that the Rohingya originated in Myanmar.
Challenging Myanmar’s narratives
The narrative publicly introduced by President Thein Sein against the Rohingya was repeatedly used by the military junta.
General Min Aung Hlaing has characterized the Rohingya as “Bengalis,” claiming that they were brought into Arakan as agricultural labourers during British colonial rule and some others entered illegally from Bangladesh.
His regime has refused to recognize the word “Rohingya” and continued labeling them as “Bengali.”
If Myanmar claims that the Rohingya are illegal Bengali migrants entered from Bangladesh, then Bangladesh could have directly asked Myanmar to show evidence on when, how, and how many alleged migrants entered Myanmar from Bangladesh.
Along with other complex political dynamics, Bangladesh’s silence until 2026 on this has created serious obstacles to resolving the Rohingya crisis.
Dhaka has now rejected Myanmar's “Bengali” label for Rohingya recently. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed said that Bangladesh does not agree with Myanmar's description of Rohingya as "Bengalis," as they have their own identity and will return to Myanmar with that identity.
Bangladesh should stick to this point directly and boldly. Bangladesh is an independent country, and its citizens enjoy their own rights and legal identity. Why would Bangladeshi people go to Myanmar?
If Myanmar claims that the Rohingya are Bangladeshi migrants who entered Myanmar illegally, it should provide credible evidence of that claim.
From 1992-2012, during the operational period of NaSaKa, Myanmar has not found a single case of illegal entrance from Bangladesh.
If millions of people had crossed from Bangladesh into Myanmar in the manner now claimed, there should be substantial evidence documenting such movement.
The absence of credible evidence for the scale of migration alleged by Myanmar should be seriously questioned by Bangladesh.
What is the verification for?
The project of verification of the Rohingya identity is a trust trap. Bangladesh never asked Myanmar about the reason for verification for the people who were one of the population groups of Myanmar -- historically, politically, and socially.
One practical source of evidence would be the population records maintained at the village level. Rohingya village administrators in Maungdaw, Buthidaung, and Rathedaung townships have their village-resident lists, and many of these administrators were appointed by the Myanmar authorities themselves.
These local records could provide valuable evidence on how many Rohingya fled from those villages. Can Bangladesh not challenge this verification game by referring to those lists? If these people are Bengali, why does Myanmar verify their identity to repatriate them?
Why has repatriation repeatedly failed?
Bangladesh and Myanmar have discussed repatriation several times and attempted to begin pilot repatriation. Yet these efforts have failed repeatedly. What conditions have made their return impossible?
First, it is often said that the situation in Arakan is “not conducive” for repatriation. But who will make the ground conducive if there is no meaningful intervention?
A conflict-affected area does not automatically become peaceful and stable without political, diplomatic, humanitarian, and security efforts to create those conditions.
In addition, for sustainable repatriation, there are important roles of the international community and regional forums such as ASEAN and OIC.
Unfortunately, while people are killed and raped, houses are burned,, the regional forums remain almost mute because of their principal of non-interference.
Second, there is currently no stable state authority capable of guaranteeing a safe return. Although Bangladesh and Myanmar have attempted to move forward with repatriation arrangements, the Myanmar junta was not honest about repatriating while they had control in northern Rakhine State until 2024.
Now the situation on the ground has dramatically changed. Much of Arakan townships are now controlled by the Arakan Army (AA) and its political wing, the United League of Arakan (ULA). Before proceeding with any realistic repatriation process, the most complicated issue is dealing with AA that controls most of the land in Arakan where the Rohingya would actually return.
Today, AA is denying the Rohingya exactly the same way junta did. Although the military and AA have been fighting as enemies, they are the same on the Rohingya issue.
Until now, a Rohingya needs a different permission letter every five miles to move within Arakan. Moreover, AA has been arresting educated Rohingya by accusing them of collaborating with the Rohingya armed groups.
Young girls and boys, even the children, are forced to work as porters and labour as well as fight in the frontline.
Bangladesh has missed the train several times. In 2024, when Myanmar's military fled here, they were treated warmly and handed over to Myanmar safely. It was a great opportunity to investigate the crisis and strategize the matter of repatriation using their testimonies.
Ultimately, the Rohingya crisis cannot be solved simply by arranging buses and sending people back across the border. Nor will it be solved by sending them to Bhashan Char.
Repatriation is not merely a physical return. It means safe, voluntary, dignified, and sustainable return with citizenship, equality, security, freedom of movement, and full rights.
For that, what we seriously need is a refugee policy.
Dr Ishrat Zakia Sultana is an Associate Professor, Sociology, North South University. Ahtaram Shin is an Independent Journalist and Editor of Rohingyatographer.

item.title: Myanmar’s forgotten war. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The Myanmar civil war is one of the clearest tests of the international community’s promise to protect civilians. Two decades on from the creation of the United Nations’ “Responsibility to Protect,” that promise has been quietly abandoned.
Myanmar has spent most of its independent life in conflict. Since its inception in 1948, it has struggled to build a political order that can hold together its highly diverse ethno-politico-religious communities. At its core is an unequal relationship between a Bamar-dominated central state and the ethnic border regions.
Military rule has defined the country’s governance. Since General Ne Win’s 1962 coup, the army -- known as the Tatmadaw -- has governed directly or through proxies. The so-called 8888 uprising of 1988 and the monk-led Saffron Revolution of 2007 were both handily crushed.
A democratic opening from 2010 to 2015 gave Aung San Suu Kyi’s National League for Democracy a landslide victory before the military seized power again in February 2021. The elections the junta staged in late 2025 and early 2026 were widely condemned as neither free nor fair.
The Responsibility to Protect
Myanmar should matter to anyone who takes the Responsibility to Protect seriously. The edict emerged from the International Commission on Intervention and State Sovereignty in 2001 and was endorsed by UN member states in 2005.
Its premise is simple: When a state cannot or will not protect its people from ethnocide, commits war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity, that responsibility passes to the international community (although this is an ambiguous entity in geopolitical terms).
Yet Responsibility to Protect provisions have always been applied selectively. Some crises attract diplomatic energy and intervention; others are treated as distant and inconvenient. A doctrine written for human protection loses its moral authority when it’s applied selectively.
Myanmar exposes this weakness. Its war draws far less western attention than Ukraine or the Middle East. Why is such an enduring and intractable conflict being treated with scant urgency?
The cost is not only battlefield deaths, but the slow attrition of refugee camps, children growing up stateless and unschooled, and people denied for years the right to return home or work.
The scale of displacement is hard to absorb. Bangladesh hosts well over a million Rohingya refugees, most in the camps of Cox’s Bazar, with roughly 150,000 more arriving since early 2024 as violence in Rakhine, a coastal state in western Myanmar, intensified in 2025-26.
Thailand shelters more than 80,000 refugees from Myanmar in nine temporary shelters along the Thai-Myanmar border.
These are not temporary inconveniences. They are long-term political failures.
Fighting the state
The Rohingya are the most visible face of this catastrophe. The 2017 exodus from Rakhine drew global attention, and Gambia’s genocide case has kept legal pressure on Myanmar.
In January 2026, the International Court of Justice held three weeks of hearings on the merits, with a judgment expected this year.
But the Rohingya are only one part of a wider conflict. For decades, ethnic armed organizations have fought the state for autonomy or territory, and many are more than armed entities.
As Prof Imtiaz Ahmed from Dhaka University has argued, some function as “proto states,” meaning they have their own currencies, control over territories and armed forces.
Most importantly, the cost of non-resolution is enormous. The five economic and cost-analysis models in the Myanmar Crisis Dashboard show that inaction carries measurable human, regional and economic consequences.
A war economy keeps the fighting alive. Rare earth mining, drug trafficking, and online scam compounds did not cause the conflict, but they sustain it. Kachin State has become central to the global rare earth supply chain and UN investigators have traced a multi-billion-dollar scam industry to the country’s lawless border zones.
How to end the conflict
If a war economy helps sustain the conflict, ending it means building something that can out-compete it. Myanmar needs peace architecture that offers an alternative to war.
One idea is a stabilization and reconstruction plan for Rakhine, among the country’s poorest regions and central to both Rohingya displacement and the wider conflict.
Justice alone has not produced safety or peace for decades. A reconstruction plan could build a peace dividend, showing that infrastructure, schools, clinics, and livelihoods can deliver more than a war economy ever will.
Such a plan would rest on three commitments. Displaced people, in the camps and the diaspora, would be trained for work so they are ready to rebuild when conditions allow. Planning should not wait for a final peace deal; negotiation and reconstruction are separate tracks that reinforce each other.
These proposals also need credible backing from donors and regional governments. The risk is that reconstruction money could be seized by the entities who profit from the war. Designing to guard against that possibility is part of the work.
Global effort required
Geopolitics cannot be ignored. China holds major stakes through the Belt and Road Initiative and hedges between the military and the armed groups; India has concerns about its northeastern frontier. The crisis is regional, not just domestic.
The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or ASEAN, must play a larger part. Its Five-Point Consensus, agreed in 2021, has not resolved the crisis and is now widely judged as a failure, yet it remains the most legitimate regional platform. The organization’s Institute for Peace and Reconciliation could study reconstruction-based alternatives.
The Responsibility to Protect cannot apply only when intervention is politically convenient. The real test isn’t how loudly governments speak when a crisis is visible, but whether they act equitably when the suffering is slow, distant and inconvenient. Myanmar is one of those tests. So far, the world is failing it.
Kawser Ahmed is an Adjunct Professor, Natural Resource Institute (NRI), University of Manitoba. A version of this article first appeared in The Conversation and is being reprinted under special arrangement.

item.title: Bulldozing 32 cannot bulldoze history. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
A few days ago, a woman named Tamanna Chowdhury Priyanka filed a petition with the Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Court as a plaintiff.
She alleged that on February 5 last year, the Bangabandhu Memorial Museum on Dhanmondi Road 32 in Dhaka was demolished after calls were made on social media, hundreds of people were mobilized, and bulldozers and excavators belonging to the City Corporation were used.
She blamed 27 people, including the then head of the interim government, Muhammad Yunus, for the destruction.
What happened next was predictable.
The court dismissed the petition, saying there was no “material” on which to accept it.
In other words, the case itself was deemed inadmissible, even before there could be any question of proving or disproving the allegations. Multiple applications naming Muhammad Yunus as a defendant have been dismissed.
However, the real issue here is not the former chief adviser. The issue is the rule of law and accountability for crimes.
During Yunus’s 18-month rule, numerous acts of violence, vandalism, arson, and mob violence were committed openly, while law enforcement agencies turned their backs on them.
One example came last December, when the offices of The Daily Star and Prothom Alo were vandalized and set on fire.
However, the nature of the case that was sought to be filed on August 20 was different from that of other incidents of mob violence.
This case concerned the destruction of one of the most important buildings in the history of Bangladesh.
The building, associated with both the glory and pain of the country, was destroyed in a planned manner, following advance notice, over three to four days and in front of the army.
History of the freedom struggle
The entire destruction, which began on February 5 last year, was broadcast live on television and across various social media platforms. No one can say they did not know what was happening; no one can say they did not know who was behind it.
But this historic building was not merely bricks and cement. It was a monument to independence, a witness to brutal murder, and a museum dedicated to the memory of the architect of the state.
Far from bringing those responsible for destroying the building to justice, there has not even been an investigation into the incident.
So why was the house at No 32 demolished? Perhaps the answer lies in the history of the building. Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s house was not simply the home of a former leader. The history of Bangladesh’s struggle for independence is inextricably linked to this house.
Mujib conducted all his activities from this house in March 1971. From the non-cooperation movement to the call for the Liberation War, crucial decisions were made from this house.
The house became a political pilgrimage site for the people. People from various professions and different parts of the country came in processions, to listen to Mujib and to tell him their stories.
Perhaps the most glorious day in the history of this building was March 23, 1971. It was Pakistan’s National Day. The Pakistani flag was supposed to be hoisted across the country.
But throughout the day, thousands of people streamed along 32 carrying the Bangladesh flag.
That day, Mujib himself hoisted the Bangladesh flag at his house, which had effectively become the administrative centre of what was then East Pakistan.
He demonstrated how independence could be proclaimed without a formal declaration of independence. Even Pakistani army officers understood the significance of that day.
The Bengali service of German state broadcaster Deutsche Welle recently published a lengthy report on 32, citing a book written by four senior Pakistani army officers stationed in East Pakistan.
“The Bengali youth were marching in the streets shouting ‘Joy Bangla’; for them it was practically an independence day,” Deutsche Welle quoted Brigadier-General Siddique Salik as writing in his book Witness to Surrender .
“That day was very significant,” the German broadcaster quoted Major General Rao Farman Ali, political adviser to the governor of East Pakistan, as saying, “It was on that day that Mujib hoisted the Bangladesh flag at his residence and declared independence.”
Black chapter
When the Pakistani army began attacking various parts of Dhaka on the night of March 25, in the initial stage of implementing its genocide plan, Mujib remained at 32.
Another chapter was added to the history of the building when he was arrested there and taken to Karachi. Preparations were made to put him on trial for treason.
Mujib’s colleagues, senior Awami League and Chhatra League leaders, had come to this building every day until the night of March 25, holding meetings, deciding on future courses of action and greeting people arriving from different parts of the country.
That night, however, the house was empty. The leaders and activists had left Dhaka for other places.
Many may not have known that within a day or two, the top leaders would enter India, meet Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, issue a formal declaration of independence, form a government-in-exile with Mujib as president, and bring the Liberation War into an organized framework with India’s assistance.
After independence, the importance of the house diminished somewhat.
Mujib himself did not leave the house to move into the official residence of the prime minister or, later, the president.
His attachment to this building would ultimately prove tragic for him. The darkest chapter in the history of the building came on August 15, 1975.
Mujib, along with almost his entire family, was killed in this building by a group of army officers and soldiers.
The image of his body lying on the stairs tells everyone what a horrific and brutal incident took place there.
The killers were granted immunity, and since then, the word “indemnity” has carried a cursed significance in Bangladeshi politics.
Vandalism and arson
The building did not remain the property of the Mujib family for very long. Nor were Awami League activities conducted from it.
Sheikh Hasina regained possession of the house from government custody in 1981. But in 1994, she and her sister Rehana established the Bangabandhu Memorial Trust and transferred the house to the trust. In other words, the house was no longer owned by Hasina and Rehana.
That same year, the “Father of the Nation Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Memorial Museum” was established in the building. The building then became national property.
But evidence that Bangladesh’s political frenzy has failed to develop a culture of preserving history emerged once again on August 5, 2024.
For the first time, amid the student-led mass uprising and the fall of the Awami League government, house No 32 was attacked, vandalized and set on fire.
At the time, it was said that members of the public, angered by Hasina’s atrocities, had attacked an establishment associated with her name. There was no functioning government in the country at the time. Although the army was responsible for maintaining law and order, it did not want to confront the angry crowd.
But what happened on February 5 last year was entirely different.
Using a speech by Sheikh Hasina to Awami League leaders and activists as a pretext, calls were made on social media to demolish the building.
People were urged to go to 32 with bulldozers. There is no way the advisers of the interim government did not know. Not even a fool would believe that the law enforcement agencies had no advance information.
The army was at 32 that day, but when the “angry crowd” arrived carrying flags bearing Arabic script and began demolishing the building, the troops withdrew.
Bulldozers and excavators were brought from the South City Corporation, and the walls and roof were torn down.
What had begun amid public anger on August 5 the previous year was completed in a cold-blooded and planned manner on February 5.
The destroyers were not merely trying to erase the memory of Bangabandhu. Their outrage was directed at the symbolic value of this building, at its moral strength. Every brick of the building bore witness to the Liberation War of 1971.
Those who demolished the building that day were not striking at Sheikh Mujib or Sheikh Hasina. The target of each blow was the memory of the Liberation War.
The current BNP government, which claimed during the election campaign to embody the spirit of the Liberation War, has remained silent about the destruction carried out during the interim government’s tenure, including the demolition of 32.
It does not appear willing to address crimes committed during the Yunus period.
But the recent attempt to bring a case suggests that demands for justice over the destruction of No 32 and other monuments associated with the Liberation War will not disappear overnight.
Sabir Mustafa is former head of BBC Bangla and is currently working as a freelance journalist and podcaster. Views expressed are the writer’s own.

item.title: Bangladesh court upholds death sentences over burning alive of teen. [ dawn ]
item.description:
DHAKA: A Bangladesh appeals court upheld on Monday the death sentence for an ex-head teacher convicted of murdering a teenage student, who was burned alive after she accused him of sexual harassment, in a case that shocked the country.

The court also maintained the death penalty for a co-conspirator in the murder of Nusrat Jahan Rafi, while 10 other defendants were acquitted. The murder of the teen, who was doused in kerosene and set on fire after she made the harassment complaint against the head of her rural religious school, horrified Bangladesh.

Nusrat suffered burns to 80 percent of her body and died in hospital four days later.

The former head teacher, SM Siraj-Ud-Dowlah, is among the two sentenced to hang. Four other defendants had their death penalties reduced to life terms by the appeals court.

Nusrat’s death triggered outrage across the nation, with protesters in the capital Dhaka staging days of demonstrations seeking “exemplary punishment” for the killers.

Published in Dawn, August 25th, 2026

item.title: Stopgaps no answer to gas crisis. [ thefinancialexpress ]
item.description:
By SYED FATTAHUL ALIM

Gas produced from rice husk as well as coal as alternative to natural gas for industries is at present under active consideration of some government leaders. Emphasis is also being laid on raising solar generation to 10,000 MW so it may support the national grid and, with storage, meet evening peak demand. Such a proposal comes at a time when factories are struggling with low gas pressure and load-shedding has also returned. As reports go, a garment factory at Dhuptara in Narayanganj is producing gas from rice husk and meeting around 70 per cent of its requirement. But the gas costs twice as much as grid gas. Now, does this offer a national solution, or merely show what a desperate factory will do to keep running?

Rice husk is no doubt a valuable biomass. Through gasification, it is heated with restricted air to produce a combustible fuel called producer gas. This can be used in boilers and for some industrial heating. But producer gas is not the same as pipeline-quality natural gas in energy content or convenience. The technology requires gasifiers, cleaning systems and trained operators to handle tar, ash and other by-products. More importantly, a factory has to secure an uninterrupted stream of husk. Paddy is harvested and milled in cycles, while its husk already has competing uses in parboiling, briquette-making, poultry bedding and household fuel. Its low bulk density makes transport and storage costly. Studies have therefore found such projects most feasible beside large rice-mill clusters where the raw material is locally available.

In that case, the Dhuptara experiment is important, but its lesson should not be overstated. Paying twice the grid-gas price may make sense when the alternative is missing an export deadline, losing buyers and leaving workers idle. Yet an emergency premium cannot become the normal energy cost of industry. Small and medium factories would be unable to buy expensive gasification equipment or maintain large husk stocks. The government may support pilot projects, common facilities in industrial clusters and research into other agricultural residues. Even so, rice husk should be treated as a local stopgap or supplementary fuel, not a universal substitute for natural gas.

The commerce  minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir's emphasis in this regard on solar power is, on the other hand, well-taken. Solar electricity cannot directly replace gas in every furnace, boiler or industrial process. But every megawatt generated from sunlight can reduce gas burnt in power plants and release more for productive industries. Solar already constitutes the overwhelming share of the country's renewable capacity, though the total remains small beside conventional generation. Reaching 10,000 MW as suggested by the minister would require an unprecedented expansion of rooftop systems, utility-scale parks, transmission facilities and battery storage. Factories, warehouses, schools and government buildings have idle roofs. These should become the first fields of the solar drive, since rooftop generation does not compete with scarce agricultural land.

Coal may similarly free some gas from power generation in the short run. However, replacing one imported fuel with another cannot be called energy security. Coal carries a heavy burden of pollution and carbon emissions, apart from exposure to international prices and shipping disruptions. In fact, no single alternative will rescue Bangladesh. 

According to the Energy Division, the country is supplying roughly 2,600 to 2,750 million cubic feet of gas a day against the 3,800 million cubic feet required to meet the shortage. Domestic fields now provide only around 1,600 million cubic feet daily. The government has plans to drill or re-drill 150 wells, connect Bhola gas with the national grid and invite international companies into offshore exploration. These plans must be pursued with deadlines, transparent contracts, modern seismic surveys and public reporting of results. Exploration carries risk and a discovery cannot start feeding factories overnight. But continued dependence on costly LNG and makeshift fuels carries a greater risk to employment, exports and foreign-exchange reserves. Rice husk may help some factories survive the present emergency and solar power can release gas for industry, but only an all-out search for new domestic gas reserves can provide a sustainable answer to the chronic crisis.

A worrying sign for remittance. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The nearly 21% month by month drop in inward remittances through mobile financial services (MFS) in June should be seen as a potential warning sign that our expat workers may not be finding it feasible to send their remittance through formal channels.
For an economy that relies so heavily on remittance inflows to stabilize foreign exchange reserves, support household consumption, and cushion external shocks, it is imperative that we do all we can to make it simpler for expat workers to send their money home.
Remittances are one of Bangladesh’s most dependable economic lifelines and when they fall, the impact is immediate: Families struggle, rural economies slow, and pressure on the balance of payments intensifies.
At a time when our country is already navigating inflation, dollar shortages, and a fragile external sector, any decline should compel policy-makers to take notice.
While we agree with experts that this is no time to sound alarm bells, and that remittance earnings may yet revert back to the highs we have become accustomed to over the past two years, it is still imperative that migrant workers are shielded from the high transfer costs, inconsistent incentives, and bureaucratic hurdles that push many toward informal channels.
When formal systems become less attractive or less reliable, remittances slip underground and deprive the economy of much‑needed foreign currency.
Ensuring stable remittance flows requires a combination of streamlined digital transfer systems and stronger outreach to migrant communities. It also demands continuous coordination between banks, MFS providers, and regulators to make formal channels faster, cheaper, and more trustworthy.
Our long‑term economic stability depends on protecting this vital source of income. Bangladesh must continue to do all it can to build confidence in formal remittance channels and ensure that the earnings of migrant workers continue to strengthen the nation.

item.title: Envisioning a modern aviation sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat stating that the government is working to hold the soft opening of Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s (HSIA) third terminal on December 16 is an encouraging sign for Bangladesh’s aviation sector.
It is a moment worth acknowledging not only because the terminal itself will be a modern, much‑needed upgrade, but because it hopefully signals a broader shift in how the country treats aviation - as a strategic national priority rather than an afterthought.
Bangladesh’s airports have struggled with congestion, outdated infrastructure, and service limitations that have held back both passenger experience and economic potential. For a nation with the aspirations we have, this simply will not do.
With rising demand for travel, expanding trade routes, and a growing expatriate population, the need for a modern aviation ecosystem has never been clearer.
Aviation is no longer just a luxury. Better airports mean smoother travel, stronger tourism, faster cargo movement, and improved global connectivity. They help exporters reach markets more efficiently, support foreign investment, and play a major role to enhance Bangladesh’s reputation as a country ready to compete in a globalized world.
As such, completing and inaugurating the third terminal must only be the beginning.
What Bangladesh needs is sustained investment in aviation, from upgrading regional airports to improving air traffic management, expanding cargo facilities, and ensuring that ground services meet international standards.
The country also needs better training, stronger regulatory capacity, and long‑term planning that anticipates future demand rather than reacts to crises.
That the minister has acknowledged this need is a positive sign, but this acknowledgement must now translate into tangible action.
A modern aviation sector is essential for a modern economy, and every step toward improving our airports is a step toward a more connected, competitive, and confident Bangladesh.

Türkiye must stop remembering South Asia through Pakistan alone. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
In June 2026, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described his visit to Dhaka as a first step towards raising Türkiye-Bangladesh relations to a strategic level. The two sides agreed on regular ministerial consultations, discussed trade and joint production, and signed an agreement on protecting cultural heritage.
A month later, Bangladesh’s army chief visited Türkiye to examine defence facilities and discuss training and technology exchange. Government ties are plainly moving forward. Turkish public awareness has not kept pace.
Pakistan occupies a special place in Türkiye’s view of South Asia. It is routinely called a brother country (“kardeş ülke” in Turkish), and that affection is neither artificial nor misplaced.
The problem is the silent assumption that Pakistan alone inherited the subcontinent’s historical solidarity with Türkiye. It did not.
When Muslims in British India supported the Turkish War of Independence, neither Pakistan nor Bangladesh existed. Bengalis were part of that mobilization.
Türkiye should therefore stop remembering South Asian Muslim support through Pakistan alone and build a reciprocal social relationship with Bangladesh, centred on historical memory, students and culture.
South Asian Muslims, including Bengalis, supported the national struggle. Bangladesh has preserved that connection unusually well. Its national poet, Kazi Nazrul Islam, wrote “Kamal Pasha” in 1921 in admiration of Mustafa Kemal. The poem entered the school curriculum. Roads in Dhaka and Chittagong carry Atatürk’s name; so do a park, a school, and a Turkish-language centre. Bangladesh has placed Türkiye in its poetry, classrooms, and public space.
The reverse is much harder to see. Bengali participation in the wider Indian Muslim campaign for Türkiye is rarely present in Turkish popular accounts. The aid is often remembered, retrospectively, as a story of Türkiye and Pakistan.
That reading compresses the geography of British India into the borders created in 1947 and treats the eastern Muslim population as an afterthought.
Pakistan and Bangladesh are not equally close to Türkiye in every policy field, nor must they be. But present-day diplomatic intensity should not determine who is allowed into historical memory.
There are understandable reasons for Pakistan’s greater visibility. Ankara and Islamabad have sustained conspicuous political, military, and diplomatic cooperation over decades. Pakistan also acts more visibly in regional security debates that attract Turkish attention.
Bangladesh has generally pursued a quieter international profile, and bilateral relations have experienced political friction, notably over the legacy of its 1971 independence.
These differences explain why Pakistan commands more attention. They do not justify turning a shared pre-partition history into an exclusively Pakistani inheritance.
This distinction matters now because official relations with Dhaka are becoming more ambitious.
Türkiye is expanding defense, trade, and humanitarian cooperation, while continuing substantial work connected to the Rohingya crisis.
Yet a relationship built mainly by ministries, defense firms, and relief agencies can remain socially thin.
Bangladesh risks appearing in Türkiye only as a market, a distant humanitarian setting or an adjunct to wider South Asian politics. Strategic language will not correct that imbalance by itself.
Turkish television has already shown how quickly cultural familiarity can grow in the other direction. Bangla-dubbed Turkish dramas have attracted mass audiences in Bangladesh; “ Kara Sevda ” reportedly captivated millions, while broadcasters developed dedicated teams of translators, scriptwriters, and voice artists.
Demand has also encouraged interest in the Turkish language. This is a major advantage, but it is still largely one-way. Bangladeshis are learning Turkish names, histories, and social codes through entertainment. Turkish audiences are learning little about Bengali life in return.
The next stage should not be another campaign that merely exports Türkiye more efficiently.
Turkish and Bangladeshi broadcasters could commission documentaries and co-productions on Kazi Nazrul Islam, Bengali support for Türkiye during the early 1920s, contemporary student life, migration, food, music, and urban change.
Turkish platforms could acquire Bangladeshi films and dramas with proper Turkish subtitles. Publishers and universities could support translations of Bengali fiction and political thought. Bangladesh’s embassy and cultural institutions also have work to do: Visibility in Türkiye cannot be produced by Ankara alone.
Bangladeshi students in Turkish universities offer the most immediate bridge. In June 2026, Bangladesh’s ambassador and Türkiye’s Presidency for Turks Abroad and Related Communities discussed expanding scholarships, training, leadership programs, and cultural exchange.
That conversation should move beyond counting scholarship recipients. Universities could fund student-led exhibitions on shared history, school visits, translation workshops, and public discussions involving Turkish classmates.
Graduates returning to Bangladesh should be connected with Turkish alumni, businesses, and cultural organizations.
Students should be supported as participants, not treated as unpaid instruments of diplomacy.
None of this requires a grand new bureaucracy. The recently signed cultural heritage agreement provides a practical opening.
A modest joint translation fund, an annual rotating public culture forum, and university grants for collaborative projects would be enough to begin.
Turkish museums, textbooks, and commemorative programs dealing with aid from Indian Muslims should explicitly include Bengal.
One accurate paragraph in a widely used exhibition may do more for mutual recognition than another official declaration of brotherhood.
Some will argue that public closeness cannot be engineered and that Pakistan’s position reflects decades of lived relations. That is partly true. Affection cannot be ordered by a ministry.
But public memory is never entirely spontaneous and is shaped by curricula, television, translations, scholarships, and commemorations. Bangladesh’s continued remembrance of Atatürk proves the point.
Giving Bangladesh a more visible place would not diminish Pakistan. Brotherhood is not a fixed quantity that one country loses when another is recognized.
The choice, then, is not between Pakistan and Bangladesh. It is between a narrow, state-centred memory of South Asia and a more accurate one.
Ankara and Dhaka are already giving their relationship strategic content. They should now give it a social foundation, beginning with the Bengalis who supported Türkiye before either modern South Asian state existed.
Until Türkiye recognizes that inheritance publicly and reciprocates Bangladesh’s cultural attention, its language of historical brotherhood will remain incomplete.
Mehmet Enes Beşer is a researcher focusing on ASEAN. His work examines Türkiye’s relations with Southeast Asian countries, particularly in the fields of economic development, industrial cooperation, and foreign policy. He's also a member of the Editorial Board of Teori magazine.

item.title: Money in the pocket, audacity on the street. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
There was a time in Bangladesh when social hierarchy was strictly dictated by the optics of wealth, lineage, and unquestioned authority.
If a member of the urban upper-middle class lost their temper and berated a street vendor, a domestic worker, or a rickshaw puller, the response was almost universally a stoic, downturned gaze.
Subservience was not merely a cultural expectation; it was an economic survival strategy.
To talk back was to risk losing one’s daily bread with zero safety net waiting on the other side. Silence was the price of survival.
Fast forward through two and a half decades of relentless economic evolution, massive expansion in export-oriented manufacturing, and the explosive growth of the informal and service sectors.
The scene on a bustling Dhaka street today looks markedly different.
When an affluent driver leans out of an SUV window to deliver a condescending lecture to a ride-sharing biker or a transport worker, the response is rarely meek silence.
It is far more likely to be a sharp, immediate, and equally vocal retort.
The lower and lower-middle classes have not suddenly vaulted into upper-income brackets, nor have they escaped the modern squeezes of inflation.
Yet, their everyday social posture has fundamentally shifted.
The long-standing silence has broken because the underlying financial calculus changed.
When a person carries even a modest degree of independent financial security, their threshold for enduring personal indignity vanishes.
The theoretical engine
This shift -- where incremental gains in real income yield a radical leap in everyday self-assertion -- reflects a profound realignment that can be mapped across economics, sociology, and political philosophy.
In economic sociology, Albert O Hirschman famously conceptualized how individuals react to unfair conditions through the dynamic of exit, voice, and loyalty.
Historically, domestic helpers or manual labourers in Bangladesh were trapped in strict loyalty because the option to exit simply did not exist.
Alternative livelihoods were scarce, and losing a patron meant immediate crisis. The economic trajectory of the last 25 years altered that equation entirely.
The growth of the readymade garment (RMG) industry, logistics networks, ride-sharing platforms, food delivery, and mobile financial services created an expanded, fluid labour market.
If a worker faces verbal abuse today, the ability to walk away -- the option to exit -- is real and viable.
That underlying freedom to leave instantly alters the dynamic of voice, providing the capacity to speak back without facing immediate catastrophe.
French sociologist Pierre Bourdieu provided another angle through his analysis of capital, distinguishing between economic capital (money and assets) and cultural capital (formal education and elite social mannerisms).
Historically, elite dominance relied on holding an absolute monopoly over both, ingraining a structural habit of deference in the working class.
Today, while an industrial supervisor or delivery driver may lack elite cultural capital, their economic capital has crossed an agency threshold.
Possessing liquid cash strips away the mystical aura of upper-class superiority; a Taka holds the exact same purchasing power at the local shop regardless of who hands it over.
Philosophically, this marks the erosion of Antonio Gramsci’s cultural hegemony, as higher real wages and technology access have unraveled the working class's passive consent to elite authority.
Regional context
When placed against regional neighbours, this Bangladeshi evolution takes on an intriguing character.
Take India and Pakistan, where feudal lineage, deep-seated caste hierarchies, and agrarian landowning power structures still cast a long shadow over every-day social interactions.
In parts of rural or semi-urban South Asia, a lower-class worker's subordination is enforced not merely by current wealth, but by centuries of entrenched social rank that money alone cannot easily wipe away.
In Pakistan's feudal belts or India's stratified interior, talking back to a social superior carries risks that extend far beyond losing a day's wage -- it can invite severe extra-economic retaliation.
In contrast, Bangladesh’s rapid post-1991 economic trajectory largely bypassed traditional feudalism, leaning heavily into a mass-market, wage-labour model driven by female-led garment employment, microfinance, and massive informal urbanization.
The Bangladeshi lower class found direct liquidity before traditional social hierarchies could formalize a modern caste-like grip.
Looking east toward Southeast Asia reveals another contrast. In countries like Vietnam or Thailand, economic empowerment among the working class evolved through different structural engines.
Thailand’s lower and lower-middle classes translated their growing economic weight into organized political voice decades ago, though social deference remains heavily codified by deep-rooted cultural and institutional norms.
In Vietnam, rapid export-led industrialization drastically raised the baseline standard of living, yet labor mobility and social assertiveness are heavily mediated through formal state structures and collectivist social organization rather than individualist friction on the street.
The Bangladeshi experience is uniquely chaotic and immediate.
Without a rigid feudal caste hierarchy holding it down from the past, or strong state-mandated social frameworks guiding it from above, empowerment in Dhaka or Chittagong manifests as raw market agency.
It is an unscripted, highly individualistic democratizing force happening in real time at bus stops, tea stalls, and traffic intersections.
The new safety net
Consider how the structure of work itself enabled this specific brand of assertiveness.
In the early 1990s, lower-class employment was overwhelmingly tied to singular, informal arrangements -- manual rickshaw pulling, agricultural u, or live-in household service -- where a worker was entirely dependent on the whims of a single master.
Financial transactions were unbanked and reliant on informal advances.
Contemporary Bangladesh presents a completely different landscape.
Today's working class operates across a diversified ecosystem of garment factories, gig-economy platforms, formal logistics, and micro-enterprises.
Mobile financial services have digitized savings and peer-to-peer transfers, providing immediate cash access without needing to beg an employer for an advance.
Furthermore, household incomes are frequently hedged by remittances from abroad or secondary family earnings.
This multi-layered safety net dramatically increases a worker's risk tolerance, giving them the confidence to push back against mistreatment without fearing instant ruin.
None of this implies that structural inequality has been dismantled, or that the working class no longer faces steep hardships in healthcare, housing, or social mobility.
A bus assistant or a factory line worker remains vulnerable to broader macroeconomic shocks and cost-of-living pressures, staying anchored within the same broad social class.
Yet, the nature of daily human interaction has been permanently rewritten.
Money in the pocket acts as a psychological shield. It transforms passive endurance into active dignity.
When personal survival is no longer strictly contingent on taking insult from an affluent neighbour or patron, the old social contract collapses.
On the modern Bangladeshi street, deference is no longer given away out of fear -- it has to be earned, because the person on the receiving end finally has the leverage to talk back.
Wafiur Rahman looks after the business desk at Dhaka Tribune.

Pakistan to host South Asian Games in April next year. [ dawn ]
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: Pakistan will host the South Asian Games from April 3 to 11 next year, 23 years after it last staged the regional sports gala in Islamabad in 2004.

The decision was taken at a meeting of the Executive Committee of the South Asia Olympic Council held here on Sunday, with Pakistan Olympic Association (POA) president Arif Saeed, who is also president of the South Asian Olympic Committee, in the chair.

The meeting reviewed preparations for the Games and approved three host cities — Islamabad, Lahore and Peshawar.

Representatives from Bangladesh, Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka attended the meeting in person, while India participated through video link. All the representatives endorsed the proposed dates, according to sources.

A visiting delegation is scheduled to inspect proposed sporting venues in Islamabad on Monday.

The Games will feature 28 sports and 346 medal events, with more than 3,200 athletes expected to participate across the three host cities. A large number of technical officials will also be part of the event, with Pakistan preparing to host around 4,000 athletes and other foreign visitors.

During Sunday’s meeting, representatives of the participating countries reviewed preparations and measures being taken by Pakistan to host the regional event.

The federal government has already given the go-ahead to the POA and other stakeholders to hold the Games and announced that the required funds would be released.

Pakistan was originally scheduled to host the Games in 2021, but the event was subsequently postponed for various reasons. Preparations are now said to be in their final stages.

The visiting delegation also visited the Taxila Museum and other historical sites on Sunday.

Sources said the Capital Development Authority (CDA), on the direction of the federal government, had started preparations to provide accommodation and other facilities to foreign visitors arriving in Islamabad next year for the South Asian Games and other international events, including the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) conference.

“The federal government has been taking every possible step to make the three international events next year in Islamabad highly successful — the South Asian Games, SCO conference and a meeting of the OIC,” a senior government official told Dawn.

He said the POA, Foreign Office and federal government were monitoring preparations to ensure that the Games were hosted successfully.

“Everyone is on board and working as a team for these Games,” he said.

Asked about India’s participation, the official said its representative had joined Sunday’s meeting through video link and endorsed the dates, which, according to him, indicated that India intended to participate.

However, another source cautioned that India’s participation could not yet be confirmed.

“India has been mixing politics with sports and has avoided visiting Pakistan. Even recently, it did not participate in a volleyball event,” the source said.

Published in Dawn, August 24th, 2026
